A notch is a small cut, groove, or indentation made into the surface or edge of something. Think of it as a deliberate bite taken out of an object — usually shaped like a V or a U, going into the material rather than sticking out of it.

If you've ever seen a piece of wood with a little triangular groove carved into its edge, that's a notch. If you've seen a belt with a row of small holes punched along its length, those individual holes and slots are often called notches too.

The key idea is: something is cut away or pressed in, leaving a small hollow mark.

In its most concrete sense, a notch is a physical marking cut into an object. Here's where you'll encounter it:

On everyday objects:

  • A belt has notches — those little slots you fasten the buckle into. When you tighten or loosen the belt, you move it to a different notch.
  • Old tallying sticks had notches carved into them to count things, like how many sheep passed by or how much grain was traded.
  • Ratchets and gears often have notches along their edges that allow a piece to click into place and hold.
  • The lapels of a suit jacket have what's called a notch lapel — the small triangular cut where the collar meets the lapel.

On screens and technology:

  • The small cutout at the top of certain smartphone screens — where the front camera sits — is called a notch. It's literally a section cut away from the display.

In tools and craftsmanship:

  • A notch in carpentry or woodworking is a cut made in a piece of wood so that another piece can fit into it snugly, like puzzle pieces locking together.
  • Arrows have a notch (sometimes spelled "nock") at the tail end — the small groove that grips the bowstring.

The unifying thread: In all these physical uses, a notch is always cut into something, it's small but deliberate, and it usually serves a functional purpose — to hold, mark, or fit something.

In geography, a notch refers to a narrow gap, pass, or opening between mountains or hills — essentially a natural "cut" through high terrain.

Franconia Notch is a famous mountain pass in New Hampshire, USA.

You can think of it as nature carving a notch into a mountain range, creating a narrow corridor through which people can travel. It's the same idea as the physical cut, just on a massive, natural scale.
The Figurative Meaning: A Step or Degree on a Scale

This is one of the most common ways you'll encounter "notch" in everyday English, especially in conversation.

Here, a notch means one step, level, or degree on some imaginary scale — a scale of quality, intensity, loudness, difficulty, or any other measurable quality.

Imagine a volume dial with markings on it. Each marking is a notch. Moving from one marking to the next is moving "a notch."

Examples:

  • "Could you turn the music up a notch?" — Make it a little louder.
  • "The spice level in this dish is a notch above what I can handle." — It's one step more intense than I can manage.
  • "After his promotion, he moved up a notch in the company hierarchy." — He rose one level.
  • "She was a notch better than the other candidates." — Slightly, but meaningfully, superior.

The scale isn't real or numbered — it's just a way of saying "a small but distinct step in one direction."

1. Top-notch
This means of the highest quality, the very best. If something is top-notch, it sits at the highest notch on the imaginary scale of quality.

"She's a top-notch surgeon."
"The hotel provided top-notch service."

You'll see this written both with and without a hyphen: top notch and top-notch. When used before a noun, the hyphen is standard.

2. A notch above / below
This means slightly better or slightly worse than something else — by exactly one degree.

"His cooking is a notch above restaurant quality." — It's slightly better than what most restaurants serve.
"The second film was a notch below the original." — It wasn't quite as good.

3. Another notch in one's belt (or a notch on one's belt)
This idiom means an achievement, a victory, or a conquest added to one's record. It comes from the old image of a hunter or soldier carving a notch into their belt or weapon for each kill or success.

"Winning this award was another notch in her belt." — It was one more achievement to add to her list.
"He treated his business wins like notches on his belt." — He collected them proudly as proof of his success.

Sometimes this phrase carries a slightly boastful or even negative connotation — the sense that the person is keeping score of people or wins like trophies.
Summary of All Meanings at a Glance

To wrap it up cleanly:

  • Physical notch: A small V- or U-shaped cut or groove made into an object's surface or edge, usually for a functional purpose (to count, to grip, to fit, to mark).
  • Geographic notch: A narrow natural gap or pass through mountains.
  • Figurative notch: One step or degree on an imaginary scale of quality, intensity, or level — used to describe small but real differences.
  • Top-notch: The absolute best, the highest quality.
  • A notch above/below: Slightly better or worse.
  • A notch in one's belt: An achievement or conquest added to one's record.

The word always carries the same underlying feeling: something precise, small, and purposeful — whether it's a physical mark, a geographic gap, or an abstract step up or down.
